title: Falling Squares
statement:
Axis-aligned squares are dropped one at a time onto a number line. Square `i` has its left edge at `left[i]` and side length `side[i]`, so it covers the half-open range `[left[i], left[i] + side[i])` along the line, and it falls straight down from above.

A square stops falling as soon as its bottom touches either the ground (height `0`) or the top of any earlier square whose horizontal range **overlaps** its own with positive length. Squares that merely touch at an edge (for example `[0, 4)` and `[4, 6)`) do **not** overlap, so the later one does not rest on the earlier one. A landed square never moves again.

After each square lands, record the height of the **tallest stack** currently on the line (the maximum top height over all squares dropped so far). Print these `n` heights in the order the squares were dropped.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `left[i]` and `side[i]`, in drop order.
outputFormat: Print `n` space-separated integers: the tallest stack height after each drop.

examples.explanation: Square 0 covers [0, 4) and has height 4. Square 1 covers [4, 6); it only touches square 0 at the edge x = 4, so it lands on the ground with top 2 and the tallest height stays 4. Square 2 covers [2, 6), overlapping square 0 (top 4) and square 1 (top 2). It rests on the higher of them, at 4, so its top is 8.
Each square lands exactly on top of the previous ones at the same position: tops at 2, 4 and 5.
The three squares are far apart, so each rests on the ground; the tallest height is always 3.

hints: When a square drops over a range, its landing height is the maximum height currently present anywhere in that range. After landing, the whole range has the same new height.
That is a range-maximum query followed by a range assignment. With coordinates compressed to the O(n) distinct edges, a segment tree with lazy assignment does both in O(log n).

An alternative is to keep the line as a sorted list of disjoint segments with a height each; a new square merges the segments it covers into one (splitting at most two partially covered ones), which is amortised O(log n) per square.
